items.title: In Israel, calls for 'unity' are a code for Jewish tribal supremacy
items.content:
In Israel, calls for 'unity' are a code for Jewish tribal supremacy
Submitted by
Orly Noy
on
Thu, 11/26/2026 - 19:43
The foundation runs deeper than a political consensus among the competing blocs: it concerns which citizens are included when they say 'we'
Former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party, waves after national election exit polls at his party headquarters in Tel Aviv, Israel, on 28 October 2026 (Shir Torem/Reuters)
Off
The saying “when fascism comes to America, it will be wrapped in a flag and carrying a cross” is commonly attributed to American novelist and playwright Sinclair Lewis.
German writer
Thomas Mann
, himself a Nobel laureate in literature, had a slightly different version: “If ever fascism should come to America, it will come in the name of freedom.”
Former Republican President Ronald Reagan, meanwhile, offered
his own version
: “If fascism ever comes to America, it will come in the name of liberalism.”
Whatever form fascism may take when it arrives in the
US
, one thing can be said with certainty: in
Israel
, it arrived in the name of unity.
It is hard to think of a word in the Hebrew language that has been more shamelessly abused than “unity” by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s inciting, divisive gang.
Take, for example, Elisha Madan, the newly elected Likud MK who has
set up
a “Unity Tent” outside the Knesset. “I intend to sit in the tent day and night, in the cold and rain, to give voice to the many people who keep reaching out to me, yearning for unity,” he declared poetically.
This great champion of unity, it is worth recalling, helped establish the
settlement of Avigail
. He was also
filmed
hurling vile slurs at the late human rights activist Ezra Nawi, who had come to the area to protect
Palestinian
residents from settler violence.
Common ground
Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, the man who warned before the election that a left-wing government would pose an
existential threat
to the state of Israel, suddenly remembered after the vote to
reach out
to his “Jewish brothers” with a call for unity.
Amir Ohana - the former Knesset speaker who boycotted the
swearing-in ceremony
of Supreme Court president Yitzhak Amit, and who
refused to allow
bereaved families into the Knesset gallery during a Netanyahu speech about the 7 October attacks, instead having them forcibly removed - also
professes
to see unity as a cherished goal, with the 26th Knesset holding the means to achieve it.
The use of the term 'the people of Israel' is no accident. It is a code word, an effective shortcut for establishing a shared sense of tribal belonging
And this week, comedian Guy Hochman
shoved
a camera rudely into MK Ahmad Tibi’s face, shouting at him: “Ahmad, unity? Unity?” This knight of unity is the same man who found the
genocide
in Gaza
particularly amusing
, and a fitting backdrop for a
stand-up performance
intended to boost the morale of the forces of destruction and annihilation.
He is also the same comedian who attended a left-wing demonstration and
declared
that its participants were “scarier than
Qatar
”. Now, he too wants
unity
.
It is easy to dismiss the unity tantrum gripping Netanyahu’s camp as a cynical ploy, designed to neutralise the meaning of its electoral defeat and spare its members the prospect of being banished to the opposition benches.
But the truth is that it rests on something much deeper, rooted in the anomaly of Israeli politics: a political landscape divided not primarily along ideological lines, but above all, over the question of support for Netanyahu.
Remove Netanyahu himself from the equation, and the common ground between the two blocs is far greater than it might appear; on many issues, their areas of agreement actually outweigh their differences.
A call for unity between two blocs that stood firmly together around the most defining event in Israel’s history since its founding - the
perpetration of genocide
against a besieged and defenceless Palestinian population - is not entirely baseless.
But the foundation of this call for unity runs even deeper than a consensus on any particular policy. It concerns the most instinctive sense of belonging shared by members of both blocs: who they mean when they say “we”.
Dangerous distinction
The Israeli right long ago replaced the concept of “Israeli citizens” with the tribal notion of “the people of Israel” - a term that clearly refers exclusively to the
Jewish collective
. This dangerous substitution is no longer confined to the right.
“The people of Israel cannot trust Netanyahu when he claims his motives are not political … We must not allow him to exploit Israel’s security to disrupt the elections,” Yair Golan, leader of the Democrats,
tweeted
about a month before the election.
The distinction between “the people of Israel” and “Israeli citizens” is anything but semantic. It reflects two fundamentally different conceptions of the Israeli collective, only one of which includes Palestinian citizens of Israel.
Why did Golan choose to invoke “the people of Israel” rather than “Israeli citizens”? Are Arab citizens of Israel not equally affected by security concerns? Do they not flee to bomb shelters - when such shelters are available to them - during wartime?
The use of the term “the people of Israel” is no accident. It is a code word, an effective shortcut for establishing a shared sense of tribal belonging and manufacturing intimacy.
How Israel’s election is further excluding Palestinian citizens from politics
Read More »
When Yashar leader Gadi Eisenkot
tells
a former Likud voter, disillusioned with Netanyahu, during an election campaign that “as far as I’m concerned, there is no way the people of Israel will not prevail,” he knows exactly what he is doing: building a sense of tribal intimacy whose boundaries are perfectly clear to both men.
It is within those boundaries that the right is now calling on him to gather under its unity campaign - boundaries that necessarily leave Arabs on the outside.
It is hardly surprising, then, that the Arab parties are the only ones presenting a civic discourse as a substantive alternative to the Jewish tribal discourse embodied in the phrase “the people of Israel”.
Here lies one of the great paradoxes of the Zionist state. Since its founding, Israel has relentlessly sought to sever the connection between Arab citizens and their Palestinian national identity, subjecting them to a process of forced “Israelisation”.
Yet the moment Arab citizens seek to give real substance to the citizenship imposed upon them after the
Nakba
, “the people of Israel” are quick to reclassify them as Palestinians and push them back beyond the boundaries of the Israeli collective. This is the declared position of at least two of the four parties that make up the so-called change bloc.
The choice now facing Eisenkot is not merely between two different governing coalitions. It is a choice between two fundamentally different conceptions of the boundaries of Israeli citizenship: between “the people of Israel” and the citizens of Israel. If he chooses the former, he will become, under cover of the “unity” discourse, a pale appendage of a fully fledged Jewish-supremacist coalition.
If he chooses the latter, he will have to accept Arab citizens as full partners in Israeli citizenship, with an equal and legitimate stake in shaping the country’s character - rather than as people whose struggle is limited to securing whatever crumbs the state is willing to throw their way.

The prime minister
has been charged with bribery, fraud and breach of trust
in three complex and overlapping criminal cases that hinge on his relationship with telecoms magnates and other wealthy businessmen. Ending the trial without a ruling
could set damaging precedents
for media independence and how politicians are held to account.

A ding-dong has divided the town of La Garnache in western France over attempts to silence the bells of the local church, which strike all night.
Since 1942, the clock tower of Notre Dame de l’Assomption has chimed an 8th-century hymn every 15 minutes … day and night. Between 10pm and 7am, the bells ring 37 times, adding up to more than 700 individual chimes.

تعثر محادثات القادة الأوروبيين حول ميزانية الاتحاد وسط خلافات بشأن الإنفاق وتمويل أوكرانيا
تعثرت محادثات قادة الاتحاد الأوروبي خلال اجتماعهم في بروكسل، الخميس، وسط خلافات بشأن الموازنة، بين توجه ألماني نحو خفض الإنفاق وربط الاتفاق بشأنها بتمويل أوكرانيا من جهة، وتمسك فرنسا بزيادة التمويل المخصص للمزارعين من جهة أخرى، إضافة لانتقادات زعيمة اليمين المتطرف مارين لوبان لمساعي إقرار خطط الإنفاق قبل الانتخابات الفرنسية المقررة العام المقبل. واستبعد رئيس الوزراء المجري التوصل إلى اتفاق خلال الاجتماع، فيما رأى نظيره الهولندي أن المفاوضات لا تزال تتطلب الكثير من العمل.

items.content:
Big lenders will aim to ‘protect their earnings’ amid temporary increase in corporation tax surcharge, says Andrew Bailey
Business live – latest updates
The governor of the Bank of England has warned that banks could look to pass on the
£1.5bn cost of Labour’s increase to tax on their profits
amid pressure on household finances.
John Healey, the chancellor, used his first budget last month to
temporarily increase the bank corporation tax surcharge from 3% to 6%
for a 15 month period from January, with the proceeds to be used to fund “breathing space” measures for households.

items.content:
Papa John’s order was made without sharing bank security details – tech that could revolutionise shopping
Retailers enter the unknown with AI shopping assistants on Black Friday
An order of Papa John’s margherita pizzas has become the first purchase in the UK to be made using an AI agent using cardless payment technology.
The order of nine mini pizzas was made as part of the Financial Conduct Authority’s (FCA) regulated sandbox trials to test the technology, using Lloyds Bank and payment specialist TrueLayer.

items.title: UN warns famine risks rising as hunger hotspots increase
items.content:
By Clara Schoenthaler
ROME, Nov 27 (Reuters) - Hunger is set to worsen significantly in 16 global hotspots over the coming six months, with famine threatening parts of Africa, two United Nations agencies warned on Friday.
The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) and World Food Programme (WFP) said Sudan, South Sudan, Somalia, northern Nigeria and Yemen faced the gravest threats, driven by conflict, displacement, economic hardship and extreme weather.

items.title: At critical juncture, Friedrich Merz finds Germans’ support for Ukraine wavering
items.content:
German chancellor is on difficult terrain, at home and abroad, as he fights to maintain European backing for Kyiv
The German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, is navigating choppy waters both at home and abroad over his insistence that Europe must keep up support – both military and financial – for Ukraine.
At a Brussels summit on Thursday, Merz reiterated his view that all EU member states – pointedly, “not 23 or 24” – should support a €45bn (£38bn) loan for Ukraine for 2027. He has
threatened to veto the bloc’s budget
unless all countries sign up to the loan, a stance that saw him accused of “classic blackmail” by Robert Fico, the populist prime minister of Slovakia. Czechia, Hungary and Bulgaria have also voiced their misgivings, to varying degrees, over Berlin’s dogged position.

items.title: Gaza’s children caught in the grip of a meningitis outbreak
items.content:
Gaza’s children caught in the grip of a meningitis outbreak
Submitted by
Hani Abu Rezeq
on
Fri, 11/27/2026 - 08:11
Contaminated water, collapse of healthcare system and scarce medical supplies are fuelling a surge in infections across the besieged enclave
Nine-month-old Mohammed, who is being treated for meningitis, sits on his mother Reham Wahdan’s lap at Al-Rantisi Hospital in Gaza City (Hani Abu Rezeq/MEE)
Off
For 10 days, two-month-old Mostafa Hallawin has been bedridden at Al-Rantisi Children’s Hospital in Gaza City.
After suffering a persistent high fever, reaching 39C, and recurring abdominal swelling, the
Palestinian
infant was diagnosed with meningitis.
“It started with a skin rash and a high fever, with his temperature reaching 39C,” his mother, Amal, told Middle East Eye.
“Every day, doctors perform medical scans and laboratory tests,” she added, saying his condition has shown little improvement, largely because of shortages of essential medicines.
Hallawin is one of the most recent children to develop meningitis amid a spike in cases across the war-torn enclave, where
Israel
has all but destroyed the healthcare system and continues to ban essential medicines.
The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (Ocha)
reported
413 suspected meningitis cases in Gaza between 27 September and 31 October, including 294 viral and 119 bacterial cases. The report said 68 percent were recorded in Gaza City.
On Tuesday, the Palestinian Health Ministry declared an "epidemic alert" across Gaza, citing a sharp rise in meningitis cases and deaths.
The ministry said 1,790 people had been diagnosed with meningitis since the beginning of the year, with 15 deaths recorded. In October alone, at least 272 infections were confirmed.
The risk of infectious diseases has increased amid overcrowded displacement shelters, unsafe drinking water, damaged sanitation systems and the collapse of essential healthcare services across Gaza.
In September, the World Health Organisation (WHO)
said
microbiological contamination in tested water samples rose from less than six percent in January to nearly 20 percent in August.
Two-month-old Mostafa Hallawin lies in a hospital bed beside his mother, Amal, at Al-Rantisi Children’s Hospital in Gaza City (Hani Abu Rezeq/MEE)
At Al-Rantisi Children's Hospital, which was heavily damaged in Israeli attacks during the war, beds are filled with children suffering from infectious diseases, including meningitis.
The growing number of cases threatens to create conditions in which infections can spread easily between children. Amal believes her child’s condition deteriorated during his hospital stay because of overcrowding and inadequate isolation facilities.
“There is little access to basic hygiene facilities, clean food and safe drinking water,” she said.
“I appeal for medicines and essential medical equipment to be allowed into Gaza for our children.
"We have lost our homes and our lives in this war. We don’t want to lose our babies too.”
Contaminated water
For Reham Wahdan, the health crisis became personal when her nine-month-old son, Mohammed, developed a high fever.
Wahdan and her family have been living alongside other displaced families in a room in the partly destroyed Islamic University building, after their home in Shujaiya, east of Gaza City, was destroyed by an Israeli attack during the
war
.
She said Mohammed's health began to deteriorate a day after they visited relatives staying in a makeshift tent near their displacement shelter.
'I appeal for medicines and essential medical equipment to be allowed into Gaza for our children'
- Amal Hallawin, Palestinian mother
She believes he got the infection from a child with meningitis whom they'd visited.
“He had suffered from a high fever for nearly a month, despite repeated attempts to give him medication to bring his temperature down,” she said.
Wahdan took Mohammed to several medical tents and treatment points, where he was given medication to reduce his fever. His temperature would fall briefly, only to rise again.
“Doctors at Al-Rantisi Hospital performed a lumbar puncture to collect a cerebrospinal fluid sample, and the test results confirmed that he had meningitis,” she said.
Wahdan also said her family had no access to safe drinking water where they were displaced.
“We drink contaminated water, and we rely entirely on distributed food,” she said.
Deteriorating conditions
Dr Nidal Ghunaim, the deputy director-general of primary health care for public health at the Ministry of Health, said both bacterial and viral meningitis cases had increased significantly compared with previous years.
He attributed much of the rise to enterovirus, which he said was closely linked to deteriorating environmental conditions across the Gaza Strip.
The contamination of drinking water with sewage had further worsened the situation, contributing to the increase in reported infections, he said.
The situation has become even more concerning following recent heavy rainfall  in Gaza.
“Many areas were flooded with rainwater, and sewage mixed with drinking water. The destruction of infrastructure has made the situation worse, and we expect that any further wave of flooding could make things much more difficult,” he told MEE.
“There are also significant shortages of laboratory supplies, medical treatments and isolation facilities in hospitals,” Ghunaim added.
He called on the international community to intervene urgently and support a comprehensive, long-term response to Gaza's environmental and water crises.
“The extensive destruction of water infrastructure has severely affected access to safe and clean water. Restoring and rehabilitating the water network must be an essential priority,” he said.
Children being treated for meningitis lie in a hospital room at Al-Rantisi Children’s Hospital in Gaza City on 14 November 2026 (Hani Abu Rezeq/MEE)
Back at Al-Rantisi Hospital, Reem Hamada has spent the past 10 days at the bedside of her five-year-old grandson, Mohammed, after he developed a high fever.
“One day, he came back from kindergarten with a high fever. We applied cool compresses to his forehead, neck and armpits to try to bring his temperature down, but it did not improve,” she said.
Throughout the interview, Mohammed lay beside her, his eyes closed, a cool compress resting on his forehead as the fever persisted.
“He is my only grandchild. What has he done to deserve this suffering?” she said.
“We are no longer living; we are as good as dead.”
Israel's genocide in Gaza
Ahmed Dremly
Gaza City, occupied Palestine

items.title: Heavy rain, wind and flooding hit much of US on Thanksgiving
items.content:
Homes without power, travel disrupted and Macy’s Thanksgiving parade postponed for first time in New York
Storms have flooded communities on the US east coast, knocking out power to nearly a million customers and prompting the first-ever postponement of Macy’s Thanksgiving Day parade in New York City.
High winds and flooding hammered both coasts, disrupting holiday travel. More than 900,000 homes and businesses were without electricity on Thursday evening, with the majority in east coast states, according to the outage tracking website PowerOutage.us. More than 2,200 flights to or from US destinations were delayed and more than 400 were cancelled, according to the flight tracking service FlightAware.

items.title: Morning update
items.content:
Morning update
Good morning Middle East Eye readers,
Here are the latest developments:
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said that its air defence system fired a warning south east of Hengam Island, forcing an American F-16 fighter jet to retreat.
US President Donald Trump has claimed that Washington does not depend on energy resources from the Middle East, and instead cites its presence to "protect" Israel and the region. "We don't use the oil. We don't need the oil. We've been there for a long time, protecting Israel and protecting the Middle East," he said. Trump added that the US has has "more oil" than any other country after Washington took over Venezuela's resources.
Trump also said that Washington will be victorious over Iran "whenever" he wants it to happen. The US president praised American forces for their role in the war on Iran, adding that they would never allow Tehran to have nuclear arms.
During a phone call, South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun assured Iranian Foreign Minister Araghchi that Seoul has "no intention of intervening in or participating in the war". Cho also indicated that there are "no plans to deploy troops to the region", according to a post on X by the Iranian Embassy in Seoul.
A number of countries and their officials have condemned the latest drone attacks launched against Kuwait, which killed two Italian nationals. Iran has denied the allegations that it launched the drones, with Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi calling the incident "suspicious".

items.content:
Watch: Israeli attack on residential building in Gaza City wounds children
An Israeli strike on a residential building in western Gaza City’s Rimal neighbourhood on Friday has injured civilians, including children and women, according to medical sources.
Gaza’s health ministry said on Thursday that Israeli attacks killed at least 19 Palestinians and wounded 48 others in the past 48 hours.
The recent attacks increased the total number of casualties since the so-called ceasefire began in October last year to 1,705.
The ministry also said a total of 74,772 people have been confirmed killed and 176,298 wounded in Gaza since Israel launched its war on 7 October 2023.

items.content:
أوكرانيا تنفي سعيها لتوسيع نطاق الحرب الروسية إلى ليبيا أو أي دولة أخرى
أكد وزير الخارجية الأوكراني أندري سيبيها، الخميس، أن بلاده لا تنوي توسيع نطاق حربها مع روسيا لتشمل ليبيا أو أي دولة أخرى، وذلك عقب إعلان كييف مسؤوليتها عن استهداف سفينتين روسيتين قبالة سواحل بنغازي، ما أدى إلى غرق إحداهما. وقال سيبيها إنه أبلغ نظيره الليبي الطاهر الباعور، بأن التحركات الأوكرانية "لم تكن موجهة ضد ليبيا أو شعبها، وإنما استهدفت أهدافا عسكرية روسية"، مؤكدا دعم بلاده الكامل لسيادة ليبيا وسلامة أراضيها والجهود الرامية إلى إعادة توحيدها.

items.title: Exclusive-US pushed Venezuela, Iraq to consider leaving OPEC, sources say
items.content:
By Ahmad Ghaddar, Ahmed Rasheed and Marianna Parraga
LONDON/BAGHDAD/HOUSTON, Nov 27 (Reuters) - The Trump administration encouraged Venezuela and Iraq to consider leaving OPEC earlier this year and prevented Venezuela from paying its annual membership dues to the group, according to ten people familiar with the matter.
The previously unreported moves targeted two of OPEC's five founding members, marking an unusually direct challenge to an organization President Donald Trump has long accused of keeping oil prices artificially high.

items.title: أستراليا تقر عقوبات لمكافحة تمويل الإرهاب بحق شخصين تشتبه في أنهما عميلان لإيران
items.content:
أستراليا تقر عقوبات لمكافحة تمويل الإرهاب بحق شخصين تشتبه في أنهما عميلان لإيران
قالت وزيرة الخارجية الأسترالية ‌بيني وانغ، في بيان، إن بلادها أصدرت، الجمعة، عقوبات مالية لمكافحة تمويل الإرهاب بحق شخصين تتهمهما بتدبير هجمات حرق متعمد معادية للسامية في سيدني وملبورن لصالح إيران. وأكدت الوزيرة أن هذه العقوبات "تعد  خطوة مهمة في سبيل عرقلة قدرة الحرس الثوري على ​تنفيذ هجمات ضد الأستراليين ومصالحهم".

items.content:
Trump argues US does not 'need the oil' from Middle East, says Washington 'protects' Israel and region
US President Donald Trump has claimed that Washington does not depend on energy resources from the Middle East, and instead cites its presence to "protect" Israel and the region.
"We don't use the oil. We don't need the oil. We've been there for a long time, protecting Israel and protecting the Middle East," he said.
Trump added that the US has has "more oil" than any other country, claiming that Washington took over Venezuela's resources.
"But what we do need is we need peace in the Middle East, because without it, you have a lot of turmoil," he added.

items.content:
What started as one artist’s response to being cut out of a music video has exploded, becoming a driving force in Nigeria’s cultural landscape
As a student in the central Nigerian city of Ilorin, Lawal Habeeb Kola loved staying in his hostel room to produce beats rather than returning to his family house in Lagos, the more frenetic city of his birth.
In 2022, one of his beats became popular on TikTok, and a version featuring ad-libbed vocals from a hypeman sent it viral. He was invited to the music video shoot in Lagos and thought his big break had finally come, but when the video was released, he was absent.

ISTANBUL, Nov 27 (Reuters) - PresidentTayyip Erdogan has formally approved theMecca Joint Defence Agreement with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia, the Official Gazette said on Friday, completing Turkey'sratification after parliament ratifiedit earlier this month.
The three countries signed a joint defence agreement in Mecca in August amid escalating concerns about the increasingly aggressive US-Israeli war against Iran and they are scheduled to hold a meeting in Islamabad on Friday and Saturday.

items.title: Trump says victory over Iran 'at hand', stresses that Tehran will 'never have a nuclear weapon'
items.content:
Trump says victory over Iran 'at hand', stresses that Tehran will 'never have a nuclear weapon'
US President Donald Trump said that Washington will be victorious over Iran "whenever" he wants it to happen.
"We have victory at hand (in Iran). It's going to be whenever, sort of, whatever I want it to be. To be honest, and we're trying to be nice, we're giving them every chance to make a deal and save a lot of lives. But I am not sure if they are going to take advantage of that," he said during Thanksgiving calls with US service members.
Trump also praised US forces for their role in the war on Iran, adding that they would never allow Tehran to have nuclear arms.
"Each of you is playing an essential role to protect not only our country today but future generations of Americans by ensuring that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon. They will never have a nuclear weapon. That I can tell you."

items.content:
University of Michigan faculty vote in support of pro-Palestine students facing charges
Nearly 60 percent of voting faculty members at the University of Michigan have backed a resolution in support of a dozen former students and staff who are now facing federal criminal charges for their participation in the 2024 anti-war encampments for Gaza.
The move is symbolic but also an indication of where much of the teaching staff stands.
On 12 November, after 2,425 members of the Faculty Senate voted on a motion stating that the Department of Justice's indictment "is part of a broader attack on both Palestine solidarity and labor unions in the United States", results showed 58.2% expressed support.
That's more than 1,000 professors, lecturers, clinicians, and other University of Michigan employees.

items.title: South Korea assures Iran that it has no plans of participating in the war
items.content:
South Korea assures Iran that it has no plans of participating in the war
During a phone call, South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun assured Iranian Foreign Minister Araghchi that Seoul has "no intention of intervening in or participating in the war".
The two exchanged views on their bilateral relations and the situation in the Middle East, discussing recent diplomatic efforts and initiatives to maintain peace and stability in the region.
According to a post on X by the Iranian Embassy in Seoul, Araghchi expressed concern regarding the "presence of any foreign military forces in the region, stressing that rather than contributing to peace and security, such a presence would heighten tensions and expand the scope of the conflict".
"Foreign Minister Cho reaffirmed South Korea’s support for peace and stability in the region, assuring Foreign Minister Araghchi that South Korea has no intention of intervening in or participating in the war and no plans to deploy troops to the region," the post added.

items.title: Yemen war: How do the rival alliances and armed factions stack up?
items.content:
Yemen war: How do the rival alliances and armed factions stack up?
Yemen, where civil war broke out in 2014, has recently been rocked by the worst fighting in years. A truce agreed in 2022 between the Ansar Allah, better known as the Houthis, who control the north, and forces loyal to the government in the south disintegrated when Saudi Arabia bombed Sanaa airport in July.
In August and September, the Houthis mounted a quick offensive, recapturing much of the western coast, including the port of Mocha, putting it within close range of ships passing the strategically important Bab el-Mandab strait.
The Houthis are now targeting Aden, Yemen’s second city and seat of its internationally recognised government since the group took the capital Sanaa 12 years ago.
Meanwhile, the Houthis have tightened their decade-long siege of Taiz, blocking the road to Aden and raising the prospect of its capture.
The Saudi-backed pro-government military coalition contains a variety of armed units and local militias, each with different goals, rival leaders and origins, leading to infighting and disorganisation.
Allegiances frequently shift and evolve: the Giants Brigade and the National Resistance Forces were each previously backed by the UAE. The leaders of both, like much of the coalition, are now bankrolled by Riyadh amid its fallout with Abu Dhabi.
With fighting spread across multiple front lines, here’s an overview of the most important military and political parties involved in the conflict.

items.title: Several countries slam suspected Iranian attack on Kuwait
items.content:
Several countries slam suspected Iranian attack on Kuwait
A number of countries and their officials have condemned the latest drone attacks launched against Kuwait, which killed two Italian nationals.
The UK minister Stephen Doughty condemned the attack as "utterly unacceptable" and said that his country "stands firmly with Kuwait, Italy and all those affected, without making mention of who could be behind the attacks.
The Syrian Foreign Ministry slammed Iran for the strikes, and affirmed its "full solidarity" with Kuwait. It also extended its condolences to the families of those killed.
Similarly, Saudi Arabia has also pinned the attacks on Iran, saying: "The continued Iranian attacks further exacerbate tensions and undermine stability."
Iran has denied the allegations that it launched the drones on Kuwait, with Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi calling the incident "suspicious".

items.title: New Zealand election: final results show ruling coalition needs minor party to govern
items.content:
Incumbent prime minister Christopher Luxon loses majority and needs support of Opportunity party to remain in power, or country faces another election
The final results of New Zealand’s general election show the incumbent rightwing coalition will need the support of a centrist newcomer party to form a government, and to avoid sending the country back to the polls.
Preliminary results
on 7 November handed the National party and its two coalition partners, the populist New Zealand First and libertarian Act parties, a slim two-seat majority,
making the election too close to call
until final votes were tallied.

items.content:
Watch: Israeli forces demolish Palestinian livestock farming community without prior notice
Israeli forces demolished approximately 50 structures, including homes and livestock shelters, in the Palestinian farming community of Samra in Tubas, in the occupied West Bank’s Jordan Valley, without issuing any prior demolition notices.
The demolitions follow a period of repeated Israeli settler attacks on the community, one of the few remaining Palestinian farming communities in the Jordan Valley.
Residents are now living in a single tent, while their livestock having been left without shelter.

Taiwanese voters go to the polls on Saturday in closely watched local elections that will shape the fortunes of the ruling Democratic Progressive party (DPP) as it navigates an increasingly precarious set of relationships on the global stage.
Saturday’s vote will choose mayors, council members and other local leaders across 22 districts. Unlike the presidential elections, in which foreign policy is often a key issue, the local elections, held
every four years

items.title: IAEA working with Russia, Ukraine on ceasefire to repair power link at Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant
items.content:
Nov 26 (Reuters) - The UN nuclear watchdog said on Thursday it was working with Russia and Ukraine to arrange a new local ceasefire at the Russian-held Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant, following another loss of offsite power.
Russian forces seized the Zaporizhzhia plant, Europe's largest with six reactors, in the first weeks of Moscow's February 2022 invasion of Ukraine.
Each side has since routinely accused the other of military activity that jeopardises nuclear safety.
The plant generates no power, but needs electricity to keep nuclear fuel cool in its reactors.

items.title: Sex, drugs, Israeli tech and Trump rivalries: Five explosive claims from Kushner-UAE book
items.content:
Sex, drugs, Israeli tech and Trump rivalries: Five explosive claims from Kushner-UAE book
An explosive new book by veteran journalist Matthew Cole claims Jared Kushner, President Donald Trump’s son-in-law and Middle East envoy, had a deep entanglement with the governments of Saudi Arabia and particularly the UAE, during the first Trump administration.
The book's most explosive claim is that Kushner was given approximately $2bn from the Saudi and Emirati governments, including $750m held at First Abu Dhabi Bank through an Emirati charity, Watani Al Emarat Foundation, ostensibly to support civic programmes in the Emirates, but in reality used for Emirati weapons purchases and covert military operations.
Kushner, who is currently acting as an envoy for Trump in Ukraine and the Middle East, has vociferously denied the claims.
But the New York Times
said
the allegations against Kushner should be investigated when Democrats take control of Congress in the new year.

items.content:
Saudi Arabia, Turkey sign two defence cooperation agreements
Saudi Arabia and Turkey have signed two memorandums of understanding aimed at strengthening cooperation in defence research, development and military technologies, according to Anadolu news agency.
The agency said the agreements were signed in Ankara on Thursday between Saudi Arabia’s General Authority for Defence Development (GADD) and two Turkish institutions: the Presidency of Defence Industries (SSB) and the Scientific and Technological Research Council of Turkey (Tubitak).
The agreements aim to expand bilateral cooperation in research, development and innovation in defence and military technologies and systems.

items.title: University of Michigan faculty vote in support of pro-Palestine students facing charges
items.content:
University of Michigan faculty vote in support of pro-Palestine students facing charges
Submitted by
MEE staff
on
Thu, 11/26/2026 - 18:42
The move comes as a dozen former students and staff face federal criminal charges over the 2024 Gaza encampments
Salma Hamamy (centre) holds a Palestinian flag at a pro-Palestinian protest during the University of Michigan's spring commencement ceremony on 4 May 2024 (Nic Antaya/Getty Images/AFP)
Off
Nearly
60 percent
of voting faculty members at the University of Michigan have backed a resolution in support of a dozen former students and staff who are now facing federal criminal charges for their participation in the 2024 anti-war encampments for Gaza.
The move is symbolic but also an indication of where much of the teaching staff stands.
On 12 November, after 2,425 members of the Faculty Senate voted on a motion stating that the Department of Justice's indictment "is part of a broader attack on both Palestine solidarity and labor unions in the United States",
results showed
58.2 percent expressed support.
That's more than 1,000 professors, lecturers, clinicians and other University of Michigan employees.
The Faculty Senate has nearly 8,000 members, but not all of them participate in voting.
On Wednesday, Faculty Senate chair Kentaro Toyama expressed his dismay that the University of Michigan Police Department was specifically called out in the resolution as having been party to the repression of students' speech.
"Even if the allegations in the resolutions were true, UMPD reports to the UM President. Unless UMPD acts in defiance of UM leadership or the ethics of law enforcement, they are following civilian orders as police norms require," Toyama wrote in an email that was viewed by Middle East Eye.
The successful resolution, he added, "concerns matters that are complex and gray".
University of Michigan still punishing pro-Palestine students after graduating
Read More »
Adi Saleem, assistant professor of Romance Languages & Literatures and Judaic Studies, introduced the resolution at the Faculty Senate's meeting earlier this month. He told MEE on Thursday that there was anti-Muslim sentiment at play, and he and another colleague were called "Nazis" afterwards by those who opposed the resolution.
"Because this resolution was moved by a Muslim professor there is obviously something antisemitic about it," he said, sarcastically.
"In the days after the resolution passed, we, the supporters of the resolution, were the focus of a right-wing and Zionist social media campaign. All of us have had our faces kind of on multiple videos accusing us of, essentially, antisemitism."
That includes assistant professor of American Culture and Digital Studies, Yarden Azoulay Katz, who told MEE that he believes the Faculty Senate chair is under both political pressure and pressure from university donors.
"Toyama's statement delivers the complete package that the university's regents, right-wing donors, and Zionist lobbying groups want to hear: that Hamas equals terrorism, that Israel has the right to exist, that Palestine is only West Bank and Gaza, and that the police keep us safe," he said.
"It also effectively says that even if the courts did not charge the defendants with vandalism or find them guilty of anything, that we know they did it and that their actions were wrong."
"It's inexcusable," he added. "Toyama has also not been upfront about the pressures being exerted on him to make such a sweeping statement."
MEE has reached out to the University of Michigan.
Prolonged punishment
The University of Michigan has continued to discipline, fire and intimidate students and staff since the 2024 protests, many of those impacted have
previously told MEE
.
As recently as this June, the FBI carried out
violent home raids
targeting students and alumni.
But the saga began long before the Trump administration assumed power in early 2025 and vowed to crack down on pro-Palestine activists and critics of Israel.
In September 2024, Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel
charged
11 students and alumni for what she described as "violent and criminal behaviour" in setting up the encampments.
By May 2025, all the charges
were dropped
, after Nessel said the cases were just not worth her office's time anymore.
Last month, however, the US Department of Justice, overseen by President Donald Trump's former personal lawyer, Todd Blanche,
indicted 12 other students
who were engaged in the 2024 anti-war protests at the University of Michigan.
US: Lieutenant criticises police report on clearing UCLA pro-Palestine encampment
Read More »
Among the charges are "conspiracy to transmit a threat to the institution", "conspiracy to tamper with a witness", and "the destruction of property to prevent seizure".
The US attorney for the Eastern District of Michigan, Jerome F Gorgon Jr, said the defendants "
terrorize Jews
".
"The main charge against them is sending messages on the internet. Really, I mean that's what it boils down to," Katz told MEE on Thursday. "They're using conspiracy charges... without needing to have
any real substantive evidence
."
"The property damage that's described in the indictment, none of it concerns federal buildings, right? So, the federal government has no business even getting into a hypothetical vandalism case here," he added.
The DOJ further alleged there was "an increased support for Hamas on college campuses" at the time of the encampments that emerged at universities across the country.
At the time
, between March and May 2024, Israel was killing up to 200 Palestinian civilians a day in its assault on Gaza, and then-President Joe Biden had
refused to use
any leverage to stop the attacks.
"If you don't stand up to this right now, there's no telling how far it could escalate," a former student-turned-employee of the university, Zainab Hakim, who is named in the indictment,
told MEE
last year.
"They are trying to paint a peaceful expression of First Amendment rights as violent in order to repress the movement," she said.
"I don't regret trying to do the right thing."
There is a legal fund that has been set up for the so-called "
Michigan 12
".

Americans celebrating Thanksgiving this year have been presented with two rather unexpected political developments: New York City's Democratic Mayor Zohran Mamdani now has control over the weather, and US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee's dogs may have acquired a second language.

items.title: Sex, drugs, Israeli tech and Trump rivalries: Five explosive claims from Kushner-UAE book
items.content:
Sex, drugs, Israeli tech and Trump rivalries: Five explosive claims from Kushner-UAE book
Submitted by
MEE staff
on
Thu, 11/26/2026 - 20:11
Emirati leader blackmailed his brother over gay sex and oversaw medical treatment that led to nerve damage, US author writes in 'Princes and Thieves'
United Arab Emirates President Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan is seen at a ceremony in Paris, France, on 19 July 2022 (AFP)
Off
An explosive new book by veteran journalist Matthew Cole claims Jared Kushner, President Donald Trump’s son-in-law and Middle East envoy, had a deep entanglement with the governments of Saudi Arabia and particularly the UAE, during the first Trump administration.
The book's most explosive claim is that Kushner was given approximately $2bn from the Saudi and Emirati governments, including $750m held at First Abu Dhabi Bank through an Emirati charity, Watani Al Emarat Foundation, ostensibly to support civic programmes in the Emirates, but in reality used for Emirati weapons purchases and covert military operations.
Kushner, who is currently acting as an envoy for Trump in Ukraine and the Middle East, has vociferously denied the claims.
But the New York Times
said
the allegations against Kushner should be investigated when Democrats take control of Congress in the new year.
The book,
Princes and Thieves: Jared Kushner and Mohamed bin Zayed’s Secret Plot to Remake the Middle East,
published last month, contains dozens of other juicy nuggets about the Middle East and the wheeling and dealing that takes place in the region. It also provides a window into the culture of the UAE’s ruling Al Nahyan family.
Cole’s sources are anonymous and MEE couldn’t independently verify all the claims but has selected several highlights below. The UAE and Saudi royal families have not commented on the claims made in the book.
Homosexual blackmail
Cole claims that in the 1990s, UAE President Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan hired two Syrians to film his brother and rival for the throne, former President Khalifa bin Zayed, having gay sex in a hotel room in southern Europe. Mohammed Bin Zayed then had Russian handlers deliver the tape to the brothers’ father - and founder of the UAE - Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan, to embarrass Khalifa.
Albania’s revolt: How Rama’s Kushner resort deal became a threat to his leadership
Read More »
Cole wrote that Zayed bin Sultan realised Mohammed was trying to blackmail his brother, but appreciated his “cunning” and was “amused”. Cole says: “Within the Al Nahyan family, Mohamed’s blackmail attempt came to be seen as an early sign of his ambition to rule the UAE."
Khalifa had only one wife and eight children, which was relatively rare for Gulf royals in the 1990s, but has become more common today.
Although Cole’s reporting on Khalifa bin Zayed’s sexual orientation has not been verified elsewhere, there are other reports of homosexuality among Gulf royals being used against them that have appeared in recent books on the Gulf.
Cole says Mohammed bin Zayed was also seen as hostile to former Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Nayef, who was eventually sidelined by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.
According to Cole, Mohammed bin Zayed lobbied the US against Mohammed bin Nayef, on the basis of his alleged homosexuality.
In the case of Mohammed bin Nayef, his sexual orientation has been reported in two well-regarded books on the Saudi kingdom: New York Times Journalist Ben Hubbard’s
MBS: The Rise to Power of Mohammed bin Salman
and
Blood and Oil: Mohammed bin Salman's Ruthless Quest for Global Power,
by journalists Bradley Hope and Justin Scheck.
Did UAE ruler drug his brother?
Khalifa bin Zayed became president of the UAE in 2004 after his father’s death. Despite his official title, he widely deferred to his brother, Mohammed bin Zayed, who was crown prince of Abu Dhabi, the UAE’s wealthiest emirate.
Epstein files: Bannon accused UAE's MBZ of 'coughing up' paedophile George Nader
Read More »
Khalifa bin Zayed’s decision to take a back seat to his ostensibly junior brother was often framed in the media as a willing decision that was eventually necessitated by a 2014 stroke he suffered.
Instead, Cole claims that he suffered from alcoholism and an “undiagnosed mental illness” long before. He says that when Mohamed bin Zayed was named deputy crown prince of Abu Dhabi in 2003, he was already providing medical treatments to his brother which left him unable to function.
“Khalifa’s medical treatment left him in a stupor, eventually causing nerve damage,” Cole wrote.
Cole suggests that Mohammed bin Zayed saw the treatment as a way to “undermine” his brother, and often forced the treatment on him with the help of an American nurse with whom he had a family connection.
According to the book, Mohammed bin Zayed had a sexual relationship with the nurse’s niece, Lisa, with whom he fathered an illegitimate child raised in Southern California.
Israeli tech inside UAE F-16s
The UAE is Israel’s closest Arab partner. The two were understood to have enjoyed close security ties for decades before the UAE joined the US-backed Abraham Accords in September 2020, making their relationship public.
DP World replaces Sultan Ahmed bin Sulayem amid UAE tycoon's links to Epstein
Read More »
The UAE has moved closer to Israel amid the US-Israeli war on Iran. The two countries are aligned in regional hotspots like Somaliland and Ethiopia as well.
Cole says that Mohammed bin Zayed was an admirer of Israel since at least the 1990s, despite his father’s reluctance to embrace Israel due to his sympathy with the Palestinians.
In 1998, after reading in Aviation Week about a new F-16 that the US had produced with Israeli software, Mohammed bin Zayed lobbied his father to purchase the warplanes. At the time, Mohammed bin Zayed was the UAE Armed Forces chief of staff and negotiated the purchase with the US.
With Mohammed bin Zayed’s backing, the UAE agreed to purchase 80 aircraft and install Israeli software in them. The decision came amid secret Israeli-Emirati discussions hosted by the Clinton Administration aimed at addressing Israel’s concerns that the sale would endanger its Qualitative Military Edge (QME).
Writer tortured to death
The UAE’s decision to move closer to Israel publicly also sparked a crackdown at home. Cole wrote that Emirati poet Habib Al Sayegh was tortured to death in 2019, after writing a column against normalisation with Israel.
Sayegh was an Emirati luminary who even defended the UAE and Saudi Arabia’s blockade against Qatar. He was very much a member of the UAE’s elite, working as an editor at the Al Khaleej newspaper and serving as secretary general of the Arab Writers Union, according to the book.
Sayegh, however, was vocal in elite circles about the UAE’s growing closeness to Israel. Despite warnings to remain silent, in August 2019 he wrote a column titled “Israel Is Our Real Enemy and A Dangerous Project”.
Following publication of the article, Sayegh was abducted from his home by security officers at the orders of Mohammed bin Zayed, Cole writes. He says he was tortured with a pair of pliers used to pull out several of his teeth by one security agent, while another whipped him with a “belt-like strap with a sharp metal piece attached”.
Sayegh was beaten for three days. When he died, one of Mohammed bin Zayed’s closest aides described his body as “almost unrecognizable,” Cole writes.
Sayegh’s dissent stood in the way of a major diplomatic deal that Mohammed bin Zayed was discussing with Kushner and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. Saudi Arabia would eventually grow cool on normalisation with Israel, but the agreement was for the Gulf states to recognise the country and sideline the Palestinians.
Jordan was envisioned as hosting the vast majority of three million Palestinians living in the occupied West Bank, thereby reducing the territory’s population by 90 percent. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu would then recognise a rump Palestinian state, Cole wrote. The state would also be awarded some land in the Negev desert and Jordanian territory.
Jared Kushner-Tom Barrack rivalry
Cole’s book not only offers a window into the lives and ambitions of Gulf rulers, but also into key figures in the Trump administration. While some of the officials are not in government today, many of them remain central officials in the Middle East.
Besides Jared Kushner, the book discusses Tom Barrack at length. Barrack, a Lebanese-American former private equity investor, is currently US ambassador to Turkey and envoy to Iraq and Syria.
Ten things Tom Barrack said in wild interview on Israel, Lebanon and Muslims
Read More »
Barrack came under fire in the first Trump administration for initiating contact between Trump and the rulers of the UAE and Saudi Arabia before he took office. The book discusses those ties at length, but also suggests that Barrack grew frustrated with Kushner’s rise in the administration.
According to Cole, Barrack wanted to create a Marshall Plan - a reference to the post-WWII fund that rebuilt Europe - for the Middle East, funded by Abu Dhabi and Riyadh, to help develop the region.
But Kushner would only permit Barrack to handle the “Egyptian part” of the Middle East. Barrack would later lobby the UAE to tell Kushner that the Gulf state wanted him as Middle East envoy.
“The message to Barrack was clear: Kushner wouldn’t share White House relationships with MBS and MBZ,” Cole wrote, referring to Mohammed bin Salman and Mohammed bin Zayed.
Barrack and Kushner clashed again when Saudi Arabia and the UAE launched a blockade against Qatar in June 2017. At the time, Riyadh and Abu Dhabi were aligned, although they have more recently fallen out over Yemen, the Iran war and the Red Sea.
Despite his business ties with Saudi Arabia and the UAE, Barrack also tried to maintain good ties with Qatar.
According to the book, when the UAE and Saudi Arabia lobbied Kushner to support the blockade, Barrack joined former Secretary of State Rex Tillerson in pressing Trump not to join.

items.title: Settlers smash foundations of Palestinian family's homes in West Bank
items.content:
Settlers smash foundations of Palestinian family's homes in West Bank
Israeli settlers smashed the foundations of two homes belonging to a Palestinian family in the occupied West Bank on Thursday, after settler attacks prevented the family from returning to them, in defiance of an Israeli court order.
Security cameras showed the settlers bringing a bulldozer to the hilltop two-storey houses on either side of a road in the village of Jaloud after midnight and spending about an hour damaging the houses. The family said it had been forced out months ago.
"This latest escalation is a direct consequence of the lack of law enforcement and the sense of impunity enjoyed by the perpetrators," said Ghiath Nasser, a lawyer representing the owners of the houses in court.
The demolition follows a surge of settler violence in which settlers have encroached on Palestinian villages, with an average of 53 settler attacks per week since the start of 2026, according to UN figures.
Reporting by Reuters

Large parts of southern and central Australia face elevated fire risk this summer, authorities say, while heatwaves and extreme temperatures are likely nationwide.
Most of Victoria, eastern Tasmania and large parts of South Australia, Western Australia, New South Wales and the Northern Territory face heightened bushfire risk – driven by high fuel loads, low soil moisture and forecast hot and dry conditions – according to the seasonal outlook from the Australian and New Zealand Council for Fire and Emergency Services (AFAC), released on Friday.

items.title: Georgian Police pepper-spray pro-Palestine Besiktas fans during match against Israeli club
items.content:
Georgian Police pepper-spray pro-Palestine Besiktas fans during match against Israeli club
A Europa League match between Besiktas and Hapoel Beer-Sheva was suspended for 30 minutes on Thursday, after police used pepper spray on pro-Palestine Besiktas fans who opened Palestine flags and banners, Turkish outlet NTV reported.
The fixture between the Turkish giants and the Israeli club is being played in Batumi, Georgia.
The match was suspended by referee Morten Krogh in the 26th minute after the police intervention, and restarted after a 30-minute delay, according to Uefa.
Anadolu Agency reported that Besiktas players joined their fans after their 2-1 victory, posing in front of a banner reading ‘Resist occupation, freedom for Palestine’.

items.title: American Doctor: Why this film isn’t what you think it’s about
items.content:
American Doctor: Why this film isn’t what you think it’s about
Submitted by
Mohamed Hashem
on
Thu, 11/26/2026 - 20:40
"American Doctor was always meant to be a decoy, a Trojan horse."
On the surface, American Doctor is a film about three American doctors who volunteered in Gaza's hospitals during Israel's war. But for director Poh Si Teng, the title was always a way in: a film to reach audiences in the West, about Palestinian health workers and the US-made bombs falling on them.
The film follows trauma surgeon Dr Feroze Sidhwa, Palestinian-American emergency physician Dr Thaer Ahmad and Dr Mark Perlmutter, from Gaza's hospitals to the halls of power in Washington.
In this Real Talk interview, Poh, Feroze and Thaer sit down with Mohamed Hashem to talk about the thinking behind the title, briefing Joe Biden on Rafah, and why funders saw the film as an "institutional risk".

items.title: Socialist weather and dogs barking in Hebrew: America's Thanksgiving culture wars
items.content:
Socialist weather and dogs barking in Hebrew: America's Thanksgiving culture wars
Submitted by
MEE staff
on
Thu, 11/26/2026 - 19:26
From Mamdani's alleged war on Thanksgiving to Mike Huckabee's dogs 'barking in Hebrew', Americans found plenty to argue about this holiday
Mayor Zohran Mamdani and NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch at a press conference following the announcement that the 100th annual Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade will be postponed, in New York City, 25 November 2026 (Bing Guan/Reuters)
Off
Americans celebrating Thanksgiving this year have been presented with two rather unexpected political developments: New York City's Democratic Mayor Zohran Mamdani now has control over the weather, and US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee's dogs may have acquired a second language.
While millions of Americans gathered with their families on Thursday, social media users were engaged in another traditional Thanksgiving activity: fighting over politics. But this time it was socialism, Islam and Zionism that took centre stage in this debate.
The
postponement
of NYC's iconic Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade because of severe weather conditions sent right-wing commentators into a frenzy, with some suggesting the decision had less to do with meteorology and more to do with Mamdani's political and religious affiliations.
It appears that, in addition to affordable housing, universal childcare and free buses, Mamdani's socialist agenda has taken over the weather in Manhattan.
Some users shared live webcam
footage
of Times Square in an apparent attempt to discredit weather forecasts, while others suggested that New Yorkers had been duped into believing the parade was called off because of rain.
For others, the mayor's Democratic Socialist background offered an alternate explanation for the storm ripping through New York.
Never mind that the parade has not actually been cancelled, but postponed until Saturday.
Gotta hand it to Mamdani. The guy killed the New York City Thanksgiving Parade for the first time in 100 years, and everyone is walking around believing that it has to do with rain.
— Abe Greenwald (@AbeGreenwald)
November 26, 2026
Unfortunately for proponents of the weather conspiracy, New York's precautions surrounding parade balloons considerably predate Mamdani's political career.
In 1997, strong winds caused a giant Cat in the Hat balloon to strike a lamppost, seriously
injuring
a spectator.
The following year, the city introduced safety regulations limiting balloon operations to sustained winds of 23mph (37kmph) and gusts of 34mph - well below the gusts of up to 65mph forecast for Thanksgiving.
The mayor responsible for introducing those measures was Republican Rudy Giuliani, which makes social media reactions like the X post depicting “the last Republican in NYC” all the more bizarre.
🇺🇸 The last republican in NYC, standing in front of Mamdani's Thanksgiving parade. One man, no tanks needed, just a mayor who postponed 100 years of tradition. #MamdaniOutNow #HappyThanksgiving https://t.co/qvnMANJmZe
— Love Majewski (@MajewskiLove1)
November 26, 2026
Philadelphia also disrupted its Thanksgiving festivities due to severe weather.
Barking in Hebrew
Meanwhile, thousands of miles away, a prominent figure on the Christian-Zionist right was celebrating Thanksgiving from Israel.
US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee
appeared
alongside his wife and their two dogs in a video expressing gratitude for the opportunity to live in the biblical land.
"What an amazing privilege it is to live here at such a consequential time. And one thing is for sure, it's never boring," Huckabee said, in a particularly jarring choice of words against the backdrop of Israel's genocide in Gaza.
One user on Reddit
wrote
, “Never boring? Yeah, because they keep killing innocent people. They get the thrill from it.”
Comedian and YouTuber Alex Stein shared a satirical video mimicking Huckabee, his wife and their dogs. In the video, Stein satirises the ambassador’s Thanksgiving message by saying, “Jesus Christ says ‘love thy neighbour, but what did Bibi Netanyahu say? Bomb thy neighbour!’” He also praises his dog for “biting four Muslim Amazon delivery drivers just this year”, adding to the ridicule.
From our family to yours, Happy Thanksgiving! 🇮🇱🦃🇺🇸 https://t.co/Gd6cshlily
— Alex Stein #99 (@alexstein99)
November 26, 2026
But the longtime supporter of Israel had another important development to share.
"Our dogs like it too, in fact, we think they now are barking in Hebrew."
The announcement left some on social media questioning whether the video was even real.
Others wondered how Huckabee's effusive praise for Israel squared with the Trump administration's much-touted "America First" agenda.
@USAmbIsrael Imagine an American sending a message on a uniquely American holiday and using it to praise Israel.
— Bill The Butcher (@317Donnely)
November 25, 2026
And so, this Thanksgiving, Americans found themselves debating the political affiliations of a weather forecast and the linguistic capabilities of two dogs.
The turkeys, at least, were largely spared the culture wars.
Israel's genocide in Gaza

Israeli attacks have killed 19 Palestinians in the past 48 hours in the Gaza Strip, Al Jazeera reported, citing the Ministry of Health.
The recent attacks increased the total number of casualties since the so-called ceasefire began in October last year to 1,705.
The ministry said a total of 74,772 people have been confirmed killed and 176,298 wounded in Gaza since Israel launched its war on 7 October 2023.

were Saif Abu Hatab, who was awaiting surgery, and Dr Rizq Abu Shaeira, a
surgeon
working at the hospital. Other surgeons, patients and their companions were among the injured.
Beyond the reporting and familiar condemnations from human rights organisations and UN agencies, the attack appeared to provoke little reaction, let alone meaningful political consequences for Israel.
But is this really surprising?

Why solidarity with Gaza failed to stop the genocide

items.content:
In a Thanksgiving post, the US president seeks investigation after blue wave of Democrats unseat Republicans
Donald Trump
has alleged without evidence that economic figures published by the US federal government before this month’s midterm elections were “fake” and demanded an investigation after voters roundly rejected his Republican party.
In a holiday message
on social media
tinged with bitterness, the US president wished a happy thanksgiving “to even those who issued fake Economic Numbers, just prior to the Election, and corrected them yesterday, three weeks late, showing that the GDP was actually 4.3%, versus 3.4%”.

items.title: Saudi Arabia says operations at refinery in Jazan halted after attack
items.content:
Saudi Arabia says operations at refinery in Jazan halted after attack
Some operations at a refinery in Saudi Arabia's Jazan region were temporarily halted after a hostile aerial projectile struck the facility on Thursday, causing a fire that was later brought under control, an official source at the Energy Ministry said in a statement carried by the Saudi Press Agency.
The attack killed a Nepalese worker and injured several people of different nationalities, the source added.

items.title: US Senate ‘permitting bill’ threatens clean water protections to speed up energy projects
items.content:
The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act passed the Senate and is now being debated in the House
An industry-backed “permitting bill”
approved by the US Senate
would gut key clean water protections with changes that would do little to speed up the development of major energy projects, advocates warn.
The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (Baaja) passed the Senate 62-33 and is now being debated in the House. The Baaja is a “permitting reform” bill that aims to reduce the time it takes federal agencies to approve major energy and infrastructure projects, like power lines, fossil fuel pipelines, natural gas plants and
datacenters
.

items.title: Oxford museum displays seized belongings of Naga freedom fighter Gaidinliu for first time
items.content:
Notebooks, clothes and ritual objects taken by British forces in India in the 1930s go on show at Pitt Rivers Museum
In 1932, British forces in north-east India imprisoned a 17-year-old girl called Gaidinliu for leading an uprising against colonial rule. While pursuing the freedom fighter through hills and valleys in the homeland of the Naga people, colonial officers also seized some of her most treasured possessions.
They were sent to the University of Oxford’s
Pitt Rivers Museum
and kept in storage. Now, for the first time, the museum is exhibiting the collection of 27 items, including a basket of Gaidinliu’s notebooks believed to contain her prophetic visions as the leader of a Naga Indigenous religion, clothes, bracelets and amulets.

items.content:
NHS chief says hospital bosses should consider asking staff and visitors to wear masks as winter pressures build
Hospitals are bracing for a “horrible spike” in flu in the coming days as winter starts to bite, the head of the NHS in England has said.
Flu and other winter viruses including Covid pose such a threat that hospital bosses should consider telling staff and visitors to wear masks, Jim Mackey said, as figures showed rates of admissions to hospital with flu were at the highest for the time of year since before Covid.

items.content:
Araghchi says Iran not behind drone attack that killed two in Kuwait
Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has rejected claims that Tehran was behind the drone attack on Kuwait.
The attack killed two Italians and injured two other people.
In a call with his Kuwaiti counterpart, Araghchi said that Iran was willing to take part in an investigation into the incident, according to Iran’s Foreign Ministry.

Israeli strikes have killed at least 16 schoolchildren in Gaza since the start of November, as young people across the territory face intensifying bombardment and a struggle to find food, clean water and shelter.
On Wednesday, Gaza’s ministry of education said: “Palestinian students had been targeted for the third time in less than 24 hours, in an escalation reflecting the continued Israeli violations against children in the Gaza Strip. The number of schoolchildren killed since the beginning of November has now risen to 16.”

items.title: Iraq closes two border crossings in Kurdistan region with Syria and Iran
items.content:
Iraq closes two border crossings in Kurdistan region with Syria and Iran
Iraqi border forces have closed two border crossings with Syria and Iran that had been administered by the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG), state media reported, as Baghdad moves to assert more control over the semi-autonomous region.
The al-Waleed crossing with Syria and the Bashta crossing with Iran, both located in territory administered by the Kurdistan region, have been closed, the commander of Iraq's border forces told the Iraqi News Agency.
The closures follow a ruling by Iraq's highest court on Wednesday allowing Baghdad to deploy federal forces along all international borders, including in the Kurdistan region.

items.title: UAE's Lana Nusseibeh says she doesn't work for the UAE
items.content:
UAE's Lana Nusseibeh says she doesn't work for the UAE
Lana Nusseibeh has a cold. “Welcome to London,” she says. This, after all, is a place where people get colds.
The Emirati diplomat has been running a relentless campaign to become the UN’s next secretary-general for more than a month now.
The race remains deadlocked. In the last informal straw poll conducted to help determine who should replace Antonio Guterres,
China
,
France
and the
UK
- who can all veto a candidate - voted to “discourage” Nusseibeh's appointment.
Perhaps sensing that the UK government’s opposition to her is fragile, Nusseibeh is in the British capital to lobby politicians and make her case to the press and civil society.

items.title: US army calls detonation of bomb chemicals in Iowa a success after fears of toxic plume
items.content:
The army blows up US stockpile of lead azide, a chemical used for explosives, to avoid uncontrollable explosion
The US army blew up the nation’s entire stockpile of lead azide, a chemical used to make explosives, saying the first checks show Wednesday’s controlled detonation in
Iowa
didn’t spread toxic dust to nearby homes and farms.
Earthen barriers were put up and foam and water were poured onto a pair of bunkers holding the 5 tons (4,500kg) of lead azide, and officials said those measures appear to have absorbed much of the blast.

items.title: Labour’s EU reset deal will be ‘floor not ceiling’, says Burnham cabinet ally
items.content:
Scottish secretary Douglas Alexander to say Britain cannot secure the change it needs ‘without changing our relationship with Europe’
Labour’s EU reset deal will be a “floor not a ceiling”, according to a close cabinet ally of Andy Burnham, who says the UK has been a “cork bobbing on the tides of history” because of the power lost by Brexit.
Douglas Alexander, the Scottish secretary, will tell a conference in Italy on Friday that the government cannot deliver the major change Britain needs “without changing our relationship with Europe. When the status quo is not working, you don’t stand still. You move forward. When the status quo is broken, you don’t ignore it. You fix it.”

items.title: Egyptians mourn, demand accountability after deadly tanker explosion kills 31
items.content:
CAIRO, Nov 26 (Reuters) - Egyptian lawmakers demanded accountability on Thursday as shocked Cairo residents mourned the deaths of 31 people in an overnight tanker explosion, the deadliest of a series of recent accidents that have stoked public anger.
The accident was caused when a car hit the back of the tanker, causing it to overturn and catch fire, public prosecutors said, adding that a suspect has been arrested.

items.title: Settlers smash foundations of Palestinian family's homes in West Bank
items.content:
By Pesha Magid
JALOUD, West Bank, Nov 26 (Reuters) - Militant Israeli settlers smashed the foundations of two homes belonging to a Palestinian family in the West Bank on Thursday, after settler attacks prevented the family from returning to them in defiance of an Israeli court order.
Security cameras showed the settlers bringing a bulldozer to the hilltop two-storey houses on either side of a road in the village of Jaloud at around 1 a.m. and spending about an hour damaging the houses. The family said it had been forced out months ago.

items.title: UK Jewish group files challenge against Hamas terror designation
items.content:
UK Jewish group files challenge against Hamas terror designation
A Jewish-led organisation has launched a challenge against
Britain’s
designation of Hamas as a terrorist organisation, arguing that it has been used to target people expressing support for
Palestinian
rights, including Jewish activists who oppose the group.
The Jewish Network for Palestine (JNP) submitted an application to the home secretary on Thursday, seeking to remove Hamas from the list of proscribed organisations under Section 4 of the Terrorism Act 2000.
The application comes five years after the UK government expanded its ban on Hamas from the group’s armed wing to the organisation in its entirety.

items.title: Turkey and Iraq close in on oil-for-construction deal to fund $16bn Development Road
items.content:
Turkey and Iraq close in on oil-for-construction deal to fund $16bn Development Road
Submitted by
Ragip Soylu
on
Thu, 11/26/2026 - 13:56
Baghdad wants to set the first stone in January with Erdogan attending, Turkish Transportation Minister Uraloglu tells MEE
An aerial photo taken in October 2022 shows the Grand Faw Port project, which is under construction in the southern Iraqi city of Basra (AFP)
Off
Turkey
and
Iraq
have finalised a deal to fund the 12,000km
Iraq Development Road
and aim to sign it before the end of the year, Turkish Transport Minister Abdulkadir Uraloglu told Middle East Eye.
Uraloglu, who met his counterparts and other senior officials in Baghdad on Wednesday, said the two sides had resolved all outstanding issues over financing the $16bn project. It was now only a matter of time before they signed the deal, he said.
“Iraq's government would like to set the first stone in January with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan present,” the minister told MEE.
First unveiled in May 2023 as a “dry canal”, the project would connect Iraq’s Grand Faw port in Basra to Turkey and Europe by rail and road, potentially adding
energy links
. It has faced several obstacles since then.
Regional officials told MEE that some of
the original partners
, including the United Arab Emirates and Qatar, were unable to provide funding, prompting Baghdad and Ankara to look for alternatives.
Uraloglu said the two sides had agreed on an oil-for-construction scheme developed by Ankara.
“We have a scheme where Iraq would sell 130,000 or 150,000 barrels of oil per day to Turkey and the money would be allocated to fund the project,” the minister said, adding that they prioritise the railway, which would require fibre optics throughout the route, allowing also a data link to be established from Basra to Turkey.
A separate Turkish official told MEE that Turkey had drawn on its experience of working with the European Union to devise a financing mechanism that could also work in other mineral-rich countries.
Under the proposed scheme, the Iraqi authorities would set the price per barrel based on market conditions. The proceeds from the oil sales would be deposited in a Turkish public bank, and a joint Turkish-Iraqi consortium would manage the funds and pay construction companies as they completed their work. Both Iraqi and Turkish firms are expected to join the undertaking of the project.
'Four-year timeline'
The official said the arrangement would make payments to contractors transparent and protect them from uncertainty over Iraq’s public finances. It would also make it harder for a change of government in Baghdad to disrupt the project and remove the need for high-interest foreign loans, the official added.
“We may even sign the finance deal next month and complete the project within a four-year timeline,” Uraloglu said.
The minister acknowledged, however, that changes in Iraq’s political leadership in the past had made it difficult to resolve outstanding issues.
Iraq resumes shipping oil for export to Turkey via pipeline
Read More »
Changes of prime minister and turnover among the ministers responsible for the project since 2023 had brought it close to cancellation.
Critics say the project has made no progress in the past three years.
One episode that drew headlines in both countries came during Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s visit to Ankara in July, when some Iraqi officials were reluctant to sign a memorandum of understanding on the Development Road.
Iraqi Transport Minister Wahab al-Hassani did not appear at the signing ceremony, leaving Erdogan visibly confused. Zaidi then intervened to ensure that the memorandum, which laid the groundwork for using oil revenues to fund infrastructure, was signed during the dinner.
Several people familiar with the matter told MEE that Iraqi Kurdish opposition to the proposed route had helped trigger the incident. Under the current plan, the railway would largely bypass Iraqi Kurdistan and reach the Turkish border near Ovakoy.
The US-Iran war
has led to a chokehold on the Hormuz strait and risked Iraq’s vital oil exports through this route, amounting to 80 percent of its total output, pushing Baghdad to review the project with fresh eyes.
“The Hormuz crisis was a wake-up call for Zaidi that he needs to focus on connectivity projects and diversify Baghdad’s export links,” Mehmet Alaca, a regional expert specialising on the Iraqi Development Road project, told MEE.
“The project in the past faced obstacles such as the intra-Iraqi government opposition and the funding issues, but this new scheme is likely to resolve it.”
However there are other problems relating to the role of the Kurds.
During Uraloglu’s visit to Baghdad, Zaidi’s government, acting on a ruling from Iraq’s constitutional court, asked the Kurdistan Regional Government to hand control of its border crossings to the central government and turn over the oil fields in areas declared as disputed under the Iraqi constitution.
Fresh tensions
The request triggered fresh tensions.
Alaca said Baghdad was angry at the Kurdish authorities, and anything, including an unwanted conflict, was on the cards.
'The Hormuz crisis was a wake-up call for Zaidi that he needs to focus on connectivity projects and diversify Baghdad’s export links'
-
Mehmet Alaca, expert
“However, there could be ways to defuse it, and a solution could be found on the development project’s route, which goes through Duhok and ends near Faysh Khabur, which is now under Iraqi Kurdish jurisdiction.
Uraloglu said Ankara would be open to minor adjustments to the railway route and additional links between the main line and stations in Iraqi Kurdistan, but that the decision rested with Baghdad.
Asked whether the tensions could delay the Development Road, a senior Turkish official said they would not affect the project in the long term.
A dispute between Kuwait and Iraq over their land and maritime boundaries has also raised questions about the plan’s viability. Uraloglu said neither Ankara nor Baghdad saw an immediate obstacle, noting that construction at Faw port was proceeding without difficulty.
Kuwait could also join the project, he said, adding that it offered potential benefits to all participants. Regional diplomats based in Ankara said Kuwait could, for example, use the route to transport oil to Turkey.
The Iraqi Development Road project could contribute $61.5bn to the Turkish economy over 10 years and create an average of 71,000 jobs a year through the siting of production and logistics centres, according to the official estimates.

items.title: Co-leader of Germany's AfD criticises planned talks with Russian envoy
items.content:
By John O'Donnell
BERLIN, Nov 26 (Reuters) - Alternative for Germany co-leader Alice Weidel has criticised an AfD lawmaker's plans to meet a Kremlin envoy, dealing a blow to Moscow's efforts to woo the opposition far-right party as Russia tries to build support for resuming gas deliveries to Europe.
Bundestag member Markus Frohnmaier is preparing to attend talks in Abu Dhabi in February or March with Kirill Dmitriev, President Vladimir Putin's top business envoy, to discuss trade, including restarting gas supplies to Germany.

items.content:
Six helipads built and feast prepared by 500 cooks for wedding hosted by Anant Singh, an MP charged with murder
It takes a brave soul to try to match
the mythic opulence
of the wedding arranged by the Indian billionaire Mukesh Ambani for his son Anant in 2024. Estimates of the cost for the months-long celebration ran to at least $600m, with world leaders and celebrities among those on the guest list.
Smaller fry though he is, Anant Singh, a legislator in India’s poorest state, Bihar, gave it his best shot on Wednesday, albeit in a rustic rural setting, for the nuptials of his daughter Shivangi Singh, and Rishikesh Kumar, an MBA student from Georgia State University in Atlanta.

items.title: Gaza hospitals receive bodies of 19 Palestinians in last 48 hours
items.content:
Gaza hospitals receive bodies of 19 Palestinians in last 48 hours
Hospitals across Gaza have received the remains of 19 Palestinians over the last 48 hours, Wafa reports, citing medical sources.
According to the report, another 48 wounded people were transferred to medical facilities for treatment.
This comes as five Palestinians, including the deputy education minister, were killed in two Israeli attacks targeting an apartment in a residential building in the central city of Deir al-Balah, and al-Shati refugee camp in Gaza's north.
At least 1,705 Palestinians have been killed and another 6,163 wounded in Israeli attacks since the so-called ceasefire took effect in October last year. Emergency teams have recovered the bodies of 851 people, but warn many more remain trapped beneath the debris.
